tier_reason: First-party criterion numbers from public bench code (benches/large_realloc.rs drives SeferAlloc, mimalloc 0.1 and System through GlobalAlloc directly), but the CPU model and rustc version are never stated (only 'Windows 10 dev machine'), so not A; no independent measurement, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README large alloc/free table (lower is better, measured 2026-07-06): 4 MiB ~58.6 ns vs mimalloc ~716 ns (~12.2x) vs System ~17.7 us (~302x); 16 MiB ~61.9 ns vs ~1.13 us (~13.5x); 64 MiB ~60.8 ns vs ~2.58 us (~33x). README 'Why bother' summarises this as ~12-35x faster than mimalloc. realloc_grow_geometric (64 B to 4 MiB) ~238 us vs mimalloc ~431 us (~1.8x; re-measured 2026-08-04 after the earlier '9.67 us / 39.6x' figure was withdrawn as physically impossible); realloc_grow_neighbour_pressure ~400 ns vs ~1.34 ms (~3,350x). The 'Up to ~18x faster than mimalloc on cached large alloc/free' wording is from the GitHub About text, not the README. README also states 0.3.0 loses to mimalloc on the cold path at small sizes (16-64 B, ~1.9-2.7x slower; 2026-07-23 run 16 B 2.37x, 256 B 2.71x slower) and on single-thread larson/mstress at T=1 (1.28-1.36x behind).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --features production; Cargo.toml [profile.bench] lto = "thin", codegen-units = 1 (Cargo default opt-level 3 for bench); mimalloc's C core is built by the mimalloc 0.1 crate's build script (Cargo.toml comment: 'at full optimization'); criterion sample_size(10), 1-2 s warm-up, 2-3 s measurement; rustc version not stated (MSRV 1.93).
corrections.hardware: One Windows 10 dev machine, CPU model not stated; README gives host noise as +-15-20 percent and up to +-60 percent run-to-run drift of absolute ns/op (ratios declared the normative signal).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1 star, 0 forks; 2,976 commits; crates.io 1,351 downloads, latest published version 0.2.1 (2026-06-30)
corrections.caveats: Headline large alloc/free ratios hold only for same-size reuse inside the decay window with a size factor of 2x or less (OPT-E cache keeps 8 committed slots); README says not to extrapolate to mixed-size or cold first-touch workloads. The win is a caching policy (pages kept committed, no OS round trip; the bench never touches the memory) rather than language or codegen; mimalloc and System return large blocks to the OS. Single Windows 10 host with unstated CPU and rustc version, quick criterion profile (sample_size 10), +-60 percent absolute drift between runs; the 16/64 MiB mimalloc/System absolute cells are carried from an earlier pre-X-arc run. The realloc_grow_geometric row was earlier published as 9.67 us / 39.6x and withdrawn on 2026-08-05 as physically impossible; the current 1.8x is the corrected figure. Commit 07a3652 (2026-10-10, 'fix(perf): restore realloc committed-span guard') restored a try_promote_to_large committed-span rejection whose empty form crashes with 0xc0000005; when the guard was emptied relative to the 2026-08-04 realloc measurement was not established. The '~18x' figure appears only in the GitHub About text (README tables give 12.2x-33x). The measured 0.3.0 tree is not on crates.io (latest 0.2.1), although the README install line asks for version 0.3. Sole author, 1 star, heavily agent-driven repo (2,976 commits, CLAUDE.md).

notes: All README table numbers match the record; baseline mimalloc (C) is measured in the same harness. Not a language-level claim: the large alloc/free and realloc wins come from SeferAlloc's committed-segment cache and in-place Large growth versus mimalloc's OS round trip and copy-and-free, so same_algorithm false stands and same_opt_level was left null (mimalloc C side built by its crate build script, Rust side thin LTO). Shortcomings to record: unstated CPU/rustc, single noisy Windows host, narrow same-size-reuse precondition, one withdrawn overstated realloc figure, crates.io lags HEAD (0.2.1).

tier_reason: README gives one first-party ratio (2.55x with mitigations disabled, 'more otherwise') against GNU Coreutils tac with no hardware, input, command, GNU version or benchmark code; the repo has no benches (Makefile bench target only runs cargo bench), so C as a number without methodology.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'significantly (2.55x if mitigations disabled, more otherwise) faster than the version of tac that ships with GNU Coreutils'. The author's blog announces the 2.0 release as up to three times faster than GNU tac (WebSearch snippet only; neosmart.net did not resolve here).
corrections.caveats: One number with no hardware, GNU tac version, input size or command; no benchmark code anywhere in the repo (top level holds only src, .cargo, Makefile; the Makefile bench target runs cargo bench but no benches exist). The blog post (neosmart.net) does not resolve from this environment; its 'up to 3x' wording is from a search snippet only. The win comes from SIMD newline search and mmap input rather than the language; piping input through stdin forces full buffering (disk spill above 4 MiB) and loses the mmap advantage. NEON path needs the nightly feature. No GitHub releases; crates.io 2.1.0 published 2024-01-22, last commit the same day.

notes: README sentence matches the record exactly; the 'more otherwise' means a larger speedup with speculative-execution mitigations on (mmap avoids read syscalls). Metadata checked: MIT, 113 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2024-01-22 (stale). Shortcomings: single unmethodical first-party ratio, no bench code, blog unreachable.

tier_reason: First-party README tables with CPU models; the public criterion benches (bench/aes_gcm.rs, chacha20_poly1305.rs, md5.rs) time only tachyon against ring and the md5 crate, while the OpenSSL column comes from an unstated separate tool with per-platform OpenSSL builds, and rustc version and target flags are not stated, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: AES-128-GCM 64 KiB, tachyon vs OpenSSL (MiB/s): Apple M4 12212 vs 11043; M1 8411 vs 8143; A16 9225 vs 7330; Snapdragon 888 4759 vs 3972; RPi4 BCM2711 56.4 vs 23.4; Ryzen Z1 Extreme 18458 vs 16407; Ryzen 9 9950X 33179 vs 33121 (tie); ring 0.17.14 is behind everywhere (9950X 15613). ChaCha20-Poly1305 64 KiB: Ryzen 9 9950X 7576 vs OpenSSL 6900 vs ring 3714; Apple M4 2855 only with the nightly tune-cpu=generic build, default build 1730 vs OpenSSL 2356 and ring 2350 (M1 default 1148 vs OpenSSL 1816, A16 default 1241 vs 1933); i7-3770 1122 vs OpenSSL 1106 while ring is 1151. MD5 beats OpenSSL on 9 of 10 platforms (e.g. Ryzen 9 9950X 1289 vs 1187), loses on Apple M4 (966 vs 982). BLAKE3 beats the blake3 1.8.2 crate on Apple and Snapdragon 888 (M4 3459 vs 2572) and loses on x86 and RPi4 (Ryzen 9 9950X 13348 vs 13441; BCM2711 347 vs 358). SHA-1 and Base64 are compared only with Rust crates (ring, data-encoding, base64).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Cargo [profile.bench] opt-level 3, lto = "fat", codegen-units 1; rustc version and target-cpu not stated (build.rs enables AVX-512 paths on Rust 1.89+ or nightly); nightly -Ztune-cpu=generic for the 'tune-cpu=generic' ChaCha20 column; OpenSSL builds (3.2.1 to 3.6.1) and how they were timed not stated.
corrections.caveats: Wins are mostly on ARM and Apple chips; on x86 it ties or loses (AES-GCM Ryzen 9 9950X tie, BLAKE3 slower on all x86 and RPi4, ChaCha20 on i7-3770 behind ring), and on Apple chips the default ChaCha20 build is 25-40 percent slower than OpenSSL and ring, winning only with nightly -Ztune-cpu=generic. The OpenSSL column is not produced by the repo's bench code (bench/*.rs compare tachyon only with ring and the md5 crate; Cargo.toml has no openssl dependency), so tachyon-vs-OpenSSL rows are cross-harness comparisons with different OpenSSL versions per platform. BLAKE3 and Base64 tables have no bench target in Cargo.toml (only aes_gcm, chacha20_poly1305, md5, sha1, sha512). README security notice: not formally audited, intended for benchmarking and experimentation, do not use in production. Recent correctness fixes (inv_bitslice byte transmutation 2026-06-01, index-initialisation race 2026-07-26) postdate an unknown measurement date. Not on crates.io (git dependency only). First-party tables only.

notes: Every number in the record matches the README; added the BLAKE3 RPi4 loss, the Apple default-build ChaCha20 losses and the missing-harness detail. Same-harness evidence exists only against ring 0.17.14, whose AES-GCM and ChaCha20 cores are BoringSSL-derived assembly (general knowledge, not re-checked here); the OpenSSL comparison is cross-tool. Shortcomings to record: x86 ties or losses, Apple ChaCha20 needs nightly tune flag, OpenSSL column outside public bench code, BLAKE3/Base64 bench code absent, unaudited crypto with a do-not-use-in-production notice.
